tagline: Gravity has no opinion about your horizontal speed
question_text: Why does a fired ball land at the same time as a dropped one?
audio_script: I am going to show you something almost everyone gets wrong. Stand on a table. Hold two identical balls, one in each hand. Drop the left ball straight down. At the same instant, fire the right ball horizontally as fast as you can. Which hits the floor first. Almost everyone says the fired ball takes longer, because it has farther to travel. Watch the animation on screen. The yellow ball is dropped. The blue ball is fired. They leave at the same instant. They fall together. Every frame of the animation shows them at the same height. The horizontal distance between them grows. The vertical position is identical. They hit the floor at exactly the same instant. The reason is that horizontal motion and vertical motion do not talk to each other. Gravity pulls downward. It has no opinion about how fast the ball is moving sideways. Write Newton's second law for each axis. The horizontal force is zero, so the horizontal acceleration is zero, so the horizontal velocity is constant. The vertical force is minus m g, so the vertical acceleration is minus g. The two equations are independent. The blue ball's horizontal motion is a straight line at constant speed. Its vertical motion is free fall. The two combine into a parabola. But they are two separate stories, joined by a single clock. This is the fundamental insight of projectile motion. Once you see it, every projectile problem becomes two easy problems instead of one hard one. Write the horizontal equation and the vertical equation. Solve each separately. Then stitch them together by eliminating time.

tagline: Work is not always force times distance
question_text: How do you add up a force that keeps changing?
audio_script: I am going to show you where calculus actually enters physics. Push a crate across a rough floor. At first it is easy. As you go, the resistance grows. By the end you are pushing with all your strength. How much work did you do. You cannot just multiply force by distance. The force kept changing. Watch the graph on screen. It shows the force as a function of position. A straight line, increasing as you go. If the force were constant, the work would be a rectangle. Height equals force, width equals distance, area equals work. But the force is not constant. So the work is not a rectangle. It is the area under the curve. How do you compute the area under a curved line. Watch the rectangles on screen. Each rectangle covers a small slice of the curve. Within that slice, the force is nearly constant. So the work in that slice is force times slice length. Add up all the rectangles. You get an approximation of the work. Now watch what happens as I add more and more rectangles. They get thinner. The approximation gets better. In the limit as the rectangles get infinitely thin, the sum becomes exact. That is the integral. Work equals the integral from a to b of F of x d x. The work done by a variable force is the area under the force-versus-position curve. This is all calculus is. It is bookkeeping for things that change. Once you have the total work, the work-energy theorem tells you what it does. The net work on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. Push with more net work than friction removes, and the object speeds up. Push with less, and it slows down. This is Newton's second law, integrated over position. Same physics, different dress.

header_title: Why the Door Handle Is Far From the Hinge
tagline: A short lever needs a bigger push
question_text: Why is the door handle placed far from the hinge?
audio_script: I am going to show you why the door handle is placed far from the hinge. Try to open a door by pushing near the hinge. It is very hard. Push near the handle, at the far edge, and the door swings open easily. The force you apply has not changed. What changed is the distance from the hinge. The quantity that matters is torque. Torque equals the force times the distance from the axis of rotation. Double the distance, and you double the torque for the same push. That is why handles are far from hinges, why wrench handles are long, and why a screwdriver bit has to fit snugly. Now watch the disk on screen. A torque of twelve newton metres is being applied. The disk starts to spin. Its angular velocity grows. The rate of growth is the angular acceleration. It depends on the torque and on the moment of inertia. The moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass. For a solid disk, it equals one half m r squared. Plug in the numbers. Four kilograms, radius zero point five metres. The moment of inertia is zero point five kilogram metre squared. The angular acceleration is torque divided by moment of inertia. Twelve divided by zero point five. Twenty four radians per second squared. That is fast. Now imagine the same torque applied to a hoop of the same mass and radius. A hoop has all its mass at the rim. Its moment of inertia is m r squared, not one half m r squared. That is twice as large. So the hoop's angular acceleration would be half. This is why the disk wins every race. It is not the mass that resists rotation. It is where the mass lives.

tagline: Why a gas gets hotter when you heat it
question_text: What does temperature actually measure?
audio_script: I am going to show you what temperature actually is. Not a number on a dial. Not a color on a thermometer. Watch the gas on screen. It looks like empty space, but it is not. It contains billions of molecules, moving in every direction, bouncing off each other and off the walls. Each molecule has a mass. Each has a speed. When we say the gas is hot, we mean the molecules are moving fast. When we say the gas is cold, we mean the molecules are moving slowly. Temperature is not a substance. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. The formula is simple. Three halves k B T equals one half m v rms squared. The left side is temperature. The right side is average kinetic energy. Double the temperature, and the average kinetic energy doubles. Not the speed. The kinetic energy. So the rms speed goes up by the square root of two. That is only about a forty percent increase. Because the energy goes as the square of the speed, not as the speed itself. Now watch what happens if we mix hydrogen and oxygen in the same box at the same temperature. The hydrogen molecules are sixteen times lighter. At the same temperature, they have the same average kinetic energy. But since they are lighter, they must move faster. Their rms speed is four times that of oxygen. This is not a small effect. It is why hydrogen escapes from the Earth's atmosphere while oxygen stays. Over billions of years, the fast hydrogen molecules at the tail end of the distribution reach escape velocity. The oxygen does not. The atmosphere we have is the one that the planet can hold on to.

tagline: Energy per unit charge
question_text: What does the label on a nine volt battery mean?
audio_script: I am going to show you what a volt actually measures. Not a force. Not a field. Energy per unit charge. Watch the sphere on screen. It carries a positive charge. Around it, there is an electric field, pointing outward. Every point in space has a direction and a strength. Now imagine carrying a small positive test charge from very far away to a point near the sphere. You have to push against the field. You have to do work. That work, per unit of charge, is the potential at that point. Near the sphere, the potential is high. Farther away, it drops. At infinity, we define it as zero. The potential of a point charge at a distance r is k Q over r. It falls off as one over r, not as one over r squared. That is one power of r slower than the field. The field is the gradient of the potential. Where the potential changes rapidly, the field is strong. Where the potential is flat, the field is weak. This is why potential is so useful. It is a scalar. One number per point, not three. It is easier to compute and easier to reason about. Around a positive charge, the potential is positive everywhere. Around a negative charge, negative everywhere. When you connect two points with different potentials using a wire, charge flows from high to low. The battery on your desk is rated at nine volts. That means every coulomb of charge that leaves the negative terminal and reaches the positive terminal has gained nine joules of energy. The battery did nine joules of work per coulomb. That is all a volt means.

tagline: Lenz law is energy conservation in disguise
question_text: Why does an induced current always oppose its cause?
audio_script: I am going to show you why an induced current always opposes its cause. This is called Lenz's law. It looks like a rule you have to memorize. It is not. It is energy conservation in disguise. Watch the coil on screen. Move a magnet toward it. A current flows. The induced current creates a magnetic field. The field from the coil pushes the magnet back. Now pull the magnet away. A current flows the other way. The induced current creates a field that pulls the magnet in. In both cases the induced current fights the change. Why. Suppose the opposite. Suppose the induced current ran the other way. Then pushing the magnet in would pull it faster. Faster magnet means more changing flux. More flux means more current. More current means a stronger pull. The system would run away. You would get more and more energy from nothing. The universe forbids this. Lenz's law is the minus sign in Faraday's equation, and that minus sign is not decoration. It is the reason the equations of electromagnetism are consistent with the laws of thermodynamics. This principle has real consequences. Move a metal plate through a magnetic field, and eddy currents form inside it. They resist the motion. This is magnetic braking, used in high-speed trains and roller coasters. Move a superconductor through a magnetic field, and the currents become perfect. The material floats. Every electromagnetic brake, every induction furnace, every electrical generator leans on this same fact. Nature fights every change.

tagline: Diffraction limits every telescope
question_text: Why is there a limit to how sharp a telescope can see?
audio_script: I am going to show you why every telescope has a fundamental limit. Point a telescope at a distant star. It should look like a single bright dot. It does not. It looks like a small disk with faint rings around it. The disk is not the star. It is the way light behaves when it passes through a circular opening. This is diffraction. Watch the pattern on screen. It is what a single bright point source looks like through a circular aperture. There is a bright central disk. Around it, rings of decreasing brightness. The angular size of the central disk depends on the wavelength of the light and on the diameter of the aperture. It is given by one point two two times lambda over D. For visible light, around five hundred nanometres, and a twelve centimetre lens, the minimum resolvable angle is about one arcsecond. That is tiny. But it is not zero. To get finer resolution, you need either a shorter wavelength or a larger aperture. This is why Mount Palomar has a five metre mirror. This is why Hubble has a two point four metre mirror. This is also why radio telescopes, which use much longer wavelengths, must be enormous. The Very Large Array in New Mexico has dishes spread across tens of kilometres. It is not a matter of engineering. It is a fundamental property of light. Rayleigh put a number on it. One point two two lambda over D. That number rules every telescope ever built. It even rules the human eye. Your pupil is about five millimetres wide. At that size, two car headlights a kilometre away are not two points. They are two overlapping blobs. You cannot resolve them. The physics is the same for a ten centimetre telescope and for a ten billion dollar space observatory.

tagline: Nothing can tell you which clock is right
question_text: Why do fast clocks run slow?
audio_script: I am going to show you one of the strangest facts in physics. A clock that moves fast runs slow. Not because it is broken. Not because it is being affected by some force. Because time itself is different for moving observers. Watch the muon on screen. It is a particle with a proper lifetime of two point two microseconds. When it is at rest in the lab, it decays in that time. Nothing we can do changes it. Now give the muon a speed close to the speed of light. Say zero point nine nine eight c. From our point of view, the muon lives much longer. Its clock is running slow. The factor is called gamma. For that speed, gamma is about sixteen. So the muon lives sixteen times longer than its proper lifetime. This is not a malfunction. This is what time does. Now here is the strange part. From the muon's own point of view, its clock is perfectly normal. It still decays in two point two microseconds. What changed is not its clock. What changed is our reference frame. Time itself dilates. It is not the same for both observers. This has been measured many times in laboratories around the world. It is why GPS satellites have to correct for it. It is why cosmic ray muons reach the ground. They should have decayed long before. But because they move fast, their internal clocks run slow, and they survive the trip. The universe has as many clocks as there are moving observers. None of them is privileged. None of them is wrong.

tagline: Mass defect equals binding energy
question_text: Why does a nucleus weigh less than its parts?
visual_data_json: [{"type":"number_line","id":"energy","range":[-30.0,30.0],"markers":[-28.3,0.0],"length":7.0,"color":"#4CC9F0"},{"type":"text","id":"note","text":"mass defect equals B.E. over c squared","pos":[0.0,5.5,0.0]}]
audio_script: I am going to show you where the missing mass went. Take a helium nucleus. Two protons, two neutrons. Weigh the four pieces separately. You get a certain mass. Now weigh the whole nucleus. It weighs less. Not by a little. By zero point zero three zero five unified mass units. Where did the mass go. It became energy. When the four nucleons came together to form the nucleus, they pulled on each other with the strong force. They fell into a deeper energy state. That change in energy had to go somewhere. It left as photons and neutrinos. By special relativity, energy has mass. The energy that left carried mass away with it. What remains is lighter. The difference is called the mass defect. The mass defect equals the binding energy divided by c squared. The energy on the left of the number line is negative. That is the binding energy. To take the nucleus apart, you have to put that energy back in. This is why fusion releases energy. Four hydrogens fuse into one helium. The helium weighs less than the four hydrogens. The missing mass becomes the energy that powers the Sun. This is why fission releases energy too. A uranium nucleus splits into lighter fragments. The fragments together weigh less than the original uranium. The difference appears as heat. Every nuclear power plant on Earth runs on this one fact. Every star in the sky burns because of it. Every time you liberate energy, some mass disappears. Every time you bind something together, mass appears. Mass and energy are the same thing, measured in different units.

tagline: No two electrons share the same state
question_text: Why do atoms fill their shells instead of collapsing?
visual_data_json: [{"type":"crystal_lattice","id":"shells","color":"#4CC9F0"},{"type":"text","id":"note","text":"each state holds at most two electrons","pos":[0.0,5.5,0.0]}]
audio_script: I am going to show you the rule that makes chemistry possible. Every electron in an atom has four quantum numbers. The principal number n tells you the shell. The orbital number l tells you the shape. The magnetic number m tells you the orientation. The spin number m s tells you which way the electron is spinning. The Pauli exclusion principle says that no two electrons in the same atom can have the same four quantum numbers. Why does this matter. Without it, every electron in every atom would fall into the lowest energy state. All atoms would look like hydrogen. There would be no chemical bonds. No molecules. No life. Watch the lattice on screen. Each site represents one quantum state. Electrons fill these sites one at a time. Two electrons can share an orbital, but only if their spins are opposite. One spin up, one spin down. That is it. The rest of chemistry follows from this single constraint. Sodium has eleven electrons. Ten of them fill the first two shells. The eleventh sits alone in the third shell. It is far from the nucleus. It is weakly held. Sodium gives it away easily. Chlorine has seventeen electrons. It needs one more to fill its outer shell. Together, sodium and chlorine make table salt. Oxygen needs two more electrons. Carbon has four. Every chemical bond, every reaction, every living cell, is a rearrangement of outer electrons under the rule that no two can share the same state. This is the deepest fact about chemistry, and it comes from a rule about quantum numbers.

tagline: Thirty and sixty give the same range
question_text: A ball launches at twenty metres per second at thirty degrees. What is its range?
audio_script: A ball launches at twenty metres per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal. What is its range. The range formula is R equals v zero squared sine two theta over g. Plug in. v zero is twenty, so v zero squared is four hundred. Sine of sixty degrees is about zero point eight six six. Divide by nine point eight. You get about thirty five metres. Notice something interesting. If you fire the ball at sixty degrees instead of thirty, you get the same range. Because sine of two theta is symmetric about forty five degrees. Thirty and sixty give the same sine. The maximum range occurs at forty five degrees, where sine of ninety is one. That is the sweet spot.

tagline: Only root two times orbital speed
question_text: What is the escape velocity from the surface of the Earth?
audio_script: What speed do you need to leave the Earth and never come back. Set the kinetic energy equal to the gravitational binding energy. One half m v squared equals G M m over R. The mass m cancels. So does the mass of the escaping object. A pebble and a rocket need the same speed. Rearrange. v equals the square root of two G M over R. Plug in the mass and radius of the Earth. You get eleven point two kilometres per second. That is about twenty five thousand miles per hour. Notice that this is the orbital speed times the square root of two. If you are already in low Earth orbit, moving at about seven point nine kilometres per second, you only need to speed up by about forty percent to escape entirely. This is why the Moon has no atmosphere. Its escape speed is only two point four kilometres per second. Too slow to hold on to gas molecules.

tagline: Moment of inertia sets the response
question_text: A torque of twelve newton metres acts on a four kilogram solid disk of radius half a metre. What is the angular acceleration?
audio_script: A solid disk of mass four kilograms and radius zero point five metres. A torque of twelve newton metres is applied. What is the angular acceleration. First find the moment of inertia. For a solid disk it is one half m r squared. Plug in four for the mass and zero point five for the radius. One half times four times zero point two five. That is zero point five kilogram metre squared. Now apply torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Rearrange. Alpha equals twelve divided by zero point five. That is twenty four radians per second squared. Notice that a hoop of the same mass and radius would have a larger moment of inertia. It would resist more. Its alpha would be half. Same torque, different response. It is all in the mass distribution.

tagline: Temperature is average kinetic energy
question_text: Hydrogen at thirty degrees Celsius has a certain rms speed. At what temperature would oxygen have the same rms speed?
audio_script: Hydrogen gas at thirty degrees Celsius has a certain rms speed. At what temperature would oxygen have the same rms speed. RMS speed is proportional to the square root of T over m. Set the two speeds equal. T H over m H equals T O over m O. Hydrogen has a molar mass of two grams. Oxygen has a molar mass of thirty two. The ratio is sixteen. So oxygen needs sixteen times the absolute temperature to reach the same rms speed. The hydrogen was at three hundred three kelvin. Multiply by sixteen. That is four thousand eight hundred and forty eight kelvin. About four thousand eight hundred and fifty. That is a very high temperature. Hot enough to glow. This is why hydrogen escapes from the atmosphere. It is light enough to reach escape speed at ordinary temperatures.

tagline: Energy per unit charge
question_text: A conducting sphere of radius zero point two metres carries a charge of one times ten to the minus seven coulombs. What is the potential at its surface?
audio_script: A conducting sphere of radius zero point two metres carries a charge of one times ten to the minus seven coulombs. What is the potential at its surface. For a charged sphere, the potential outside is the same as if all the charge were concentrated at the centre. V equals k Q over R. k is nine times ten to the ninth. Q is one times ten to the minus seven. R is zero point two. Plug in. Nine times ten to the ninth times one times ten to the minus seven is nine hundred. Divided by zero point two is four thousand five hundred. So the potential at the surface is four thousand five hundred volts. Inside the sphere, the potential is the same everywhere. It does not change. Because the electric field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero. No field means no change in potential. The charge, all of it, sits on the surface.

tagline: Electrons drift slower than a snail
question_text: A copper bar with a cross section of zero point five square centimetres carries ninety eight amperes. What is the drift velocity of the electrons?
audio_script: A copper bar. Cross section zero point five square centimetres. Current ninety eight amperes. What is the drift velocity of the electrons. Current equals n e A v d. Rearrange. v d equals I over n e A. For copper, n is about eight point five times ten to the twenty eight electrons per cubic metre. e is one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs. A is zero point five square centimetres, which is five times ten to the minus five square metres. Plug in. v d equals one point four times ten to the minus four metres per second. That is zero point one four millimetres per second. A snail moves faster. Yet the light comes on instantly. Why. Because the electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light. It pushes all the electrons along at once. The signal is fast. The carriers are slow.

tagline: Below it nothing ejects
question_text: Potassium has a work function of two electron volts. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject an electron?
audio_script: Potassium has a work function of two electron volts. What is the longest wavelength of light that can eject an electron. At the threshold, the energy of the photon exactly equals the work function. h c over lambda equals phi. Solve for lambda. h is six point six three times ten to the minus thirty four. c is three times ten to the eighth. Phi is two point zero times one point six times ten to the minus nineteen. That is six point two four times ten to the minus seven metres. Six hundred twenty four nanometres. That is deep red. Longer wavelengths, in the infrared, cannot eject electrons from potassium. No matter how bright the light is. Brightness does not matter. Only frequency. This is why Einstein's photon model replaced the wave model of light.

tagline: Missing mass becomes binding energy
question_text: A helium four nucleus has a mass of four point zero zero one five unified mass units. What is its binding energy?
audio_script: A helium four nucleus. Two protons plus two neutrons. If you add the masses separately, you get four point zero three two unified mass units. The actual helium nucleus weighs four point zero zero one five. Difference. Zero point zero three zero five unified mass units. Multiply by nine hundred thirty one point five MeV per unified mass unit. That gives about twenty eight point four MeV. Divide by four nucleons. About seven MeV per nucleon. Helium four is unusually tightly bound. This is why it is the endpoint of fusion in stars. Every heavy element in your body started as helium. Fused together by the heat of dying suns.

tagline: Second law is statistical not mechanical
question_text: Why do the gas molecules in a box never spontaneously return to one corner?
audio_script: Watch the gas particles on screen. They start in the left half of the box. They bounce around. Within a second they have spread through the whole box. Now ask a strange question. Could they all spontaneously return to the left half. The equations of motion are reversible. Every collision could be run backward. So in principle, yes. In practice, you would wait longer than the age of the universe. The number of ways to arrange the particles in the left half is astronomically smaller than the number of ways to spread them out. The system evolves toward the more numerous arrangements. Not because it is forced to. Because it is overwhelmingly more likely. This is the second law of thermodynamics. It is not a law of mechanics. It is a statistical near-certainty. And it gives the universe its arrow of time.

tagline: Two up, one down
question_text: A proton is made of two up quarks and one down quark. What is its electric charge?
audio_script: A proton is made of three quarks. Two up quarks. One down quark. Up quarks carry a charge of plus two thirds of the elementary charge. Down quarks carry minus one third. Add them up. Plus two thirds plus two thirds minus one third. That is plus one. The proton's charge is exactly plus e. Notice how the fractional charges combine into an integer. You never see a quark in isolation. They always come in twos and threes. The strong force binds them so tightly that trying to pull one out just creates new quark pairs. This is called confinement. And it is why we only ever see integer charges in nature.
